Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Marcus Heller is a 49-year-old architect, married, who presented for treatment following a traumatic incident he witnessed approximately fourteen months ago. He describes a period of gradual deterioration that has finally, in his own words, "made it impossible to keep pretending things are fine."

The event occurred on a Saturday afternoon when Marcus was visiting a construction site in an urban neighborhood to review progress on a mixed-use development he had designed. Walking back toward his car along a side street, he witnessed a brutal assault — a man being beaten by two attackers in an alley between two buildings. The violence was prolonged and close. Marcus froze at the mouth of the alley, unable to move or intervene, watching the attackers use their fists and then a length of pipe. He remembers the sound of impact, the smell — a combination of garbage from a nearby dumpster and something metallic and biological he could not name at the time — and the sight of the victim's body going limp on the concrete. The attackers fled past him. He stood there for what he later learned was nearly eight minutes before he called 911.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself unable to account for the sequence of what he had seen. When he tried to reconstruct it — whether for the police, or later for his wife — the pieces came out of order, or large portions simply were not there. More distressing still was a quality he struggled to articulate even to himself: he knew what had happened, he had been present, and yet when he sat across from his wife at dinner and she asked him how he was doing, the words for what he carried would not come. He would open his mouth and find nothing. She began to interpret his silences as withdrawal. He had no way to correct her impression.

When the memories did surface, they did not feel like recollections. They felt immediate and present — the smell especially, which could be triggered by something as ordinary as a garbage truck passing his office building on collection days, or by the iron-tinged air near a construction site, environments he had once moved through without a second thought. His stomach would lurch before his mind caught up, nausea arriving as a kind of early warning system his body had installed without his consent. Any sudden movement in his peripheral vision — a colleague gesturing too quickly, a door swinging open — sent a spike of alarm through him that he found deeply embarrassing in professional settings.

Marcus had come to believe, in a way he could not fully justify but also could not dislodge, that something intrinsic to him had placed him at that alley at that moment — that he was, in some essential way, the kind of person to whom terrible things happen and who fails to act when it matters. He felt set apart from colleagues and friends who moved through the world with what seemed to him an unearned ease. At work, this had concrete consequences. He had stopped conducting site visits alone, rerouting that responsibility to junior staff with explanations that sounded professional but were driven by the fact that he could not enter a building without first locating every exit, could not sit in a meeting room without positioning his chair against the wall where he could see the door. His firm's open-plan studio, which he had once championed, had become a daily ordeal. A senior partner had noted his disengagement in a recent review.

At home, his wife had stopped asking about the incident. The silence between them had thickened into something neither of them addressed directly.

What finally brought Marcus in was a presentation he was required to give in a glass-walled conference room on the fourteenth floor of a downtown building — a room with no wall behind the presenter's position. He stood at the front, felt the exposure at his back, and could not begin. He excused himself and did not return. He called for an appointment the following morning.

What he most fears, he said quietly at intake, is that nothing about him will ever feel safe again. What he hopes, with considerably less certainty, is that he is wrong.
